q: You are sailing from Paros to Naxos on this heading. What point of sail are you on?
a: Broad reach
why: Wind on the quarter, about 135° off the bow, is a broad reach.

q: The genoa and main are sheeted in hard and you cannot steer any closer to the wind. What point of sail is this?
a: Close-hauled
why: Close-hauled is the closest course to the wind that keeps the sails full, about 45°.

q: You were close-hauled and have borne away a little to this heading. What point of sail are you on now?
a: Close reach
why: Between close-hauled (45°) and a beam reach (90°) is a close reach.

q: You settle on this heading for the long leg down to Kos. Where do you set the mainsail, and what is the main risk?
a: Eased right out; an accidental gybe
o: Sheeted in hard; the sails stalling
Centred; the boat going into irons
Half out; the boat tacking by itself
why: On a run the main is eased fully, and a wind shift or wave can swing the boom across.

q: You have just borne away from close-hauled onto this heading. What do you do with the sheets?
a: Ease both until the sails just stop luffing
o: Pull both in harder to keep the speed
Leave them — the sails trim themselves
Ease the main and pull in the genoa
why: As you bear away, ease the sheets: trim each sail to the edge of luffing.

q: You were close-hauled on 045°. Now the sails start to lift and flap. What has happened and what do you do?
a: You are headed: bear away to keep the sails full
o: You are lifted: luff up and point higher
Nothing has changed: hold your heading
You are headed: ease the sheets and hold course
why: A veer of 20° puts 045° inside the no-go zone; bear away or tack.

q: The skipper calls "luff up 20 degrees". What heading do you steer?
why: Luffing up turns the bow towards the wind: 090° − 20° = 070°.

q: You bear away 45° from this heading. What is your new heading and point of sail?
a: 270°, beam reach
why: Bearing away turns from the wind: 315° − 45° = 270°, wind now on the beam.

fig.note: Close-hauled, heading 315°, wind from the north

q: Your boat tacks through 90°. After tacking from this heading, what course will you be steering?
why: Close-hauled 45° each side of a northerly wind: 315° tacks to 045°.

fig.note: Close-hauled, heading 315°, wind from the north

q: You need to know which tack you are on. On this heading, what is it?
a: Port tack
o: Neither — you are on a reach
why: The tack is named after the side the wind comes over; tacks apply on every point of sail.

q: You are on a dead run with the main boom out to starboard. Which tack are you on?
a: Port tack
o: No tack — the wind is dead astern
Whichever side the genoa is on
why: On a run the tack is the side opposite the main boom.

fig.note: Dead run, main boom to starboard

q: The skipper asks where the other yacht is. How do you call it?
a: Abeam to starboard
why: Abeam is 90° from the bow; starboard is the right-hand side facing forward.

q: A ferry is coming up from this direction to overtake you. How do you call its position to the crew?
a: On the starboard quarter
why: The quarter is about 45° abaft the beam, between the beam and the stern.

q: Your lookout spots a fishing boat here. How should she call it out?
a: On the port bow
why: The bow is about 45° either side of dead ahead; port is the left side.

q: A small motorboat is close to your heading line, a little to the right. How do you report it?
a: Fine on the starboard bow
why: "Fine" means close to the bow line; "broad" means nearer the beam.

q: A RIB is following in your wake. Where is it?
a: Dead astern
why: Directly behind the stern is dead astern.

q: You and another yacht are sailing side by side. Which boat is the windward boat?
a: The other yacht
o: Whichever boat is on starboard tack
why: The windward boat is the one nearer the wind, upwind of the other.

q: You are on the foredeck facing aft, towards the cockpit. Which side of the boat is port?
a: On your right
why: Port is the left side when facing forward, so it is on your right when you face aft.

q: The skipper asks you to lay the passerelle "fore-and-aft" on the side deck. How do you place it?
a: Lengthways, along the boat
o: Across the boat, side to side
why: Fore-and-aft means lengthways, bow to stern; athwartships means across.

q: A crew member feels seasick and wants to be sick over the side. Which side do you send them to?
a: Port, the leeward side
o: Over the transom, behind the helm
why: Always to leeward, downwind, so it blows away from the boat.

q: A gust heels the boat hard. The skipper calls "everyone to windward!". Where does the crew sit?
a: Port side, the high side
o: In the middle of the cockpit
Down below, on the saloon sole
why: Windward is the side the wind comes from; crew weight there reduces heel.

q: Reversing into the berth, the skipper calls "helm amidships!". What do you do?
a: Centre the wheel so the rudder is straight
o: Steer for the middle of the gap
Hand the wheel to the crew in the middle
why: Amidships on the helm means the rudder is centred, in line with the keel.

q: You are sailing along this coast towards the next harbour. What is it called, and how far off do you keep?
a: A lee shore; keep well off
o: A weather shore; keep well off
A lee shore; close in for shelter
A weather shore; close in for flat water
why: A lee shore has the wind blowing onto it; a failure there drives you onto the rocks.

q: You are trimming the genoa on this winch. The skipper calls "ease the genoa". What do you do?
a: Let the sheet out a little, under control
o: Wind the sheet in a little
Roll the genoa away a little
Take the sheet off the winch
why: To ease is to let a line out gradually; to trim or sheet in is to pull it in.

q: Before a tack, the skipper asks you to put two turns of the lazy sheet on a winch. Which line do you load?
a: The unused one on the windward side
o: The loaded one on the leeward side
The furling line for the genoa
why: The lazy sheet is the one not working; it becomes the working sheet after the tack.

q: You call "lee-ho" and turn the boat. When does the crew release the old genoa sheet?
a: As the bow comes through the wind
o: Once settled on the new tack
why: Too early and the genoa flogs; too late and it is backed and stops the turn.

q: Your destination is upwind, to the north-west. Which manoeuvre puts you on the other close-hauled course?
a: Tack: turn the bow through the wind
o: Gybe: turn the stern through the wind
why: Changing from one close-hauled course to the other means tacking.

q: You are outside the harbour and about to hoist the mainsail under engine. How do you point the boat?
a: Head to wind, motoring slowly
why: Head to wind the sail does not fill or snag while it goes up.

q: At check-in you find a bent post holding up the guardwires next to the cockpit. Which part is damaged?
a: A stanchion
why: Stanchions are the posts that carry the guardwires along the deck.

q: The bow navigation lights on your yacht are fixed to the steel rail around the bow. What is that rail?
a: The pulpit
why: The pulpit is the rail at the bow; the pushpit is the rail at the stern.

q: The dinghy outboard is clamped to a bracket on the steel rail around the stern. What is that rail?
a: The pushpit
why: The pushpit (stern rail) surrounds the cockpit at the stern.

q: A big following sea is starting to break into the cockpit. Which opening do you close so it cannot flood the cabin?
a: The companionway, with the washboards
why: Washboards close the companionway; the cockpit drains must stay open to empty it.

q: Your charter yacht has a deep fin keel with a bulb. Compared with a long-keeled boat, how does she handle?
a: Turns tightly but tracks less steadily
o: Can dry out upright on a beach
Heels less and needs no ballast
why: A short fin pivots easily; a long keel holds a straight course.

q: A friend's boat sits upright on the mud at low tide in her UK harbour. What keel does she most likely have?
a: Twin (bilge) keels
o: A fin keel with a bulb
why: Twin keels let a boat take the ground upright; fin and long keels fall over.

q: Your yacht has twin rudders and a wide stern. Heeled over upwind, what do they give you?
a: The leeward rudder stays deep and keeps grip
o: The boat can turn in its own length
Strong prop wash over both rudders
why: A single central rudder lifts out as a wide boat heels; the lee rudder of a pair stays in.

q: Your charter yacht has twin rudders and one central propeller. Manoeuvring slowly in the marina, what do you notice?
a: Little steering until she has way on
o: Prop wash kicks the stern very hard
She pivots on the spot like a cat
Steering astern is easier than ahead
why: The rudders are off-centre, out of the prop wash, so they only work with water flowing past.

q: Water drips into the cabin where a shroud passes through the deck. Which fitting is leaking?
a: The chainplate
why: Shrouds are anchored to chainplates that pass through the deck to the hull.

fig.title: Below decks, after rain
lines: Drip from the deckhead beside the saloon
Directly under where a shroud meets the deck

q: You roll the genoa away with the furling line. Which wire does the sail wrap around?
a: The forestay
why: A roller-furling genoa rolls round a foil over the forestay.

q: At check-in you find damage on this wire. What is it and what do you do?
a: A shroud: report it and do not sail
o: A shroud: tape it and sail gently
A halyard: turn it end for end
The forestay: keep the genoa furled
why: Shrouds hold the mast up sideways; a damaged one can bring the rig down.

fig.title: Check-in: rig
lines: Wire from the mast to the side deck
Three strands broken at the lower end
Boat due to leave in an hour

q: At check-in you see a split pin missing from the threaded fitting at the foot of a shroud. What is the fitting and what do you do?
a: A bottlescrew: fit and tape a new pin
o: A gooseneck: leave it, it needs no pin
A clutch: tape over the gap
A chainplate: tighten it by hand
why: Bottlescrews (turnbuckles) adjust the rigging; without a pin they can unscrew.

q: The mainsail has chafe marks halfway up, where it rubbed on the struts sticking out sideways from the mast. What rubbed it?
a: The spreaders
why: Spreaders hold the shrouds out from the mast; downwind the main presses on them.

q: The pin joining the boom to the mast has worked loose. Which fitting is it?
a: The gooseneck
why: The gooseneck is the hinge between the boom and the mast.

q: On your fractional-rigged yacht the wind is building. What does pulling on the backstay adjuster do?
a: Bends the mast and flattens the main
o: Makes the main fuller and more powerful
Lifts the boom and opens the leech
Moves the genoa sheet car forward
why: Backstay tension bends a fractional mast, flattening the main and tightening the forestay.

q: Close-hauled on starboard tack, a windward shroud parts with a bang. What do you do at once?
a: Tack, to put the broken side to leeward
o: Luff up head to wind and stop
Ease all sheets and hold the course
why: Tacking takes the load onto the intact leeward shroud before the mast falls.

q: Beating up to Hydra, the forestay fitting breaks at the bow. Which way do you turn?
a: Bear away onto a run
o: Hold course and ease the main
why: Running puts the wind load on the backstay and takes it off the forestay.

fig.title: Forestay failure
lines: Forestay pulled out at the stemhead

q: You are bending on the genoa at check-in. To which corner do you attach the sheets?
a: The clew
why: The clew is the lower aft corner, where the sheets go.

q: Putting in a slab reef, you hook the reef cringle at the front of the sail onto the hook by the gooseneck. Which cringle is it?
a: The tack cringle
why: The new tack goes on the reefing hook; the reef line pulls the new clew to the boom.

q: The back edge of the genoa vibrates with a buzzing noise. Which edge is it and what fixes it?
a: The leech: tighten the leech line a little
o: The luff: tighten the genoa halyard
The foot: ease the genoa sheet
The leech: ease the sheet right out
why: The leech is the trailing edge; the leech line stops it fluttering.

q: A batten falls out of its pocket as you hoist the main. What will the sail lack without it?
a: Support for the curved leech
o: A mark for the reef points
why: Battens hold out the roach, the curve of the leech beyond a straight line.

q: Your charter yacht has an in-mast furling main and the wind is rising. How do you reduce it?
a: Ease the outhaul and wind in the furling line
o: Lower the halyard and tie in the reef points
Tighten the outhaul and ease the furling line
Roll the sail round the boom
why: The main rolls into the mast; keep a little outhaul tension so it rolls tightly.

q: Your new charter boat has a self-tacking jib. What does the crew do with the jib sheet when you tack?
a: Nothing — it crosses on its own track
o: Release it and winch in the other sheet
Ease it fully before the tack
Move the car to the new side by hand
why: A self-tacking jib has one sheet on a track across the foredeck.

q: You drop the main and it falls neatly into the bag on the boom. Next morning, hoisting, the battens catch on lines either side. What helps?
a: Point head to wind and watch the battens
o: Hoist on a reach so the sail fills
Tighten the lazy jacks hard first
Pull the kicker on before hoisting
why: The lazy jacks guide the sail down; head to wind the battens clear them.

q: On a dead run in light wind the genoa keeps collapsing behind the main. What can you do?
a: Goose-wing it on the opposite side
o: Sheet the genoa in hard amidships
why: Set the genoa on the side away from the main, ideally held out by a pole.

q: Upwind in 18 knots, the lower part of the main is too full and the boat heels. Which line do you pull?
a: The outhaul
why: Outhaul tension flattens the foot of the main and depowers it.

q: As the wind rises the deepest part of the main moves back towards the leech. Which control pulls it forward again?
a: The cunningham
why: More luff tension (cunningham or halyard) moves the draft forward.

q: You are about to drop the main for the night. The boom is not held up by a rigid vang. What do you do first?
a: Take up the topping lift
why: The topping lift holds the boom up so it does not fall into the cockpit or bimini.

q: Close-hauled, the boom rides high and the main leech stays loose even with the mainsheet hard in. What is the likely cause?
a: The topping lift is still tight
why: A tight topping lift holds the boom up; ease it once the sail is hoisted.

q: Close-hauled in a gusty F5, the boat heels hard in each gust. Which quick move depowers the main?
a: Let the traveller down to leeward
o: Pull the traveller up to windward
Ease the outhaul to make it fuller
why: Dropping the traveller opens the main's angle to the wind without changing its shape.

q: The halyard is in a clutch, loaded by the hoisted main. You need to ease it. What do you do before opening the clutch?
a: Put it on a winch and take the load
o: Open the clutch and hold the tail
Pull the halyard tail tight by hand
why: Opening a loaded clutch lets the line run; the winch must hold it first.

q: The wind has risen to 25 knots and you must roll the genoa away. How do you handle the sheet?
a: Ease it slowly, keeping some tension
o: Let it run free, then furl
Keep it cleated while you furl
why: A little sheet tension stops the sail flogging and rolls it tightly.

q: During slab reefing, which line pulls the new clew down to the boom?
a: The reefing line
why: Each reef has its own clew line (pennant) led along the boom.

q: Close-hauled in a rising Meltemi, you decide to reef the main. What do you ease before lowering the halyard?
a: The mainsheet and the kicker
o: The genoa sheet and the traveller
The topping lift and the backstay
why: Easing the main spills wind; easing the kicker lets the boom rise as the sail comes down.

q: You are leaving the harbour at Mykonos with this forecast. When do you reef?
a: Before you leave the shelter of the harbour
o: When the rail first goes under
Only if the genoa will not furl
why: Reef early: it is easiest in sheltered water before the wind arrives.

q: The wind has dropped and you want to shake out the reef. What is the right order?
a: Untie the ties, ease the reef line, then hoist
o: Hoist, then untie the ties and reef line
Ease the reef line, hoist, then untie the ties
Tighten the kicker, then hoist hard
why: Hoisting against tied reef points tears the sail.

q: Close-hauled, you check the genoa telltales. Which way do you move the sheet car?
a: Forward
why: If the top luffs first the leech is too open; moving the car forward closes it.

q: Steering close-hauled, you watch the genoa telltales. Which way do you steer?
a: Bear away a little
why: Windward telltales lifting mean you are pinching; bear away until they stream.

q: On a beam reach, you watch the genoa telltales. What do you do with the sheet?
a: Ease it until both stream
why: A fluttering leeward telltale means the sail is stalled: over-sheeted.

q: On a beam reach the sails are pinned in tight, the boat heels and slows. What is happening?
a: The sails are stalled: over-sheeted
o: The boat is about to gybe
why: Sheeted too tight for the course, the airflow breaks away and drive drops.

fig.title: Beam reach
lines: Main and genoa sheeted in hard

q: The top leech telltale on the main keeps disappearing behind the sail. What do you do?
a: Ease the mainsheet or kicker a little
why: A hidden top telltale means the leech is too closed and stalled; twist it open.

q: A light F2 breeze on a flat sea, beam reaching to Antiparos. How do you set the main?
a: Fuller: ease the outhaul a little
o: Flat: outhaul and cunningham hard on
Reefed, to keep the boat upright
Boom hard down with the kicker
why: Light wind wants a fuller sail; flatten it as the wind rises.

q: Reaching in a gusty F6, you want the top of the main to spill the gusts by itself. What do you adjust?
a: Ease the kicker a little to let it twist
o: Tighten the kicker to stop any twist
Pull the traveller up to windward
Ease the outhaul to make it fuller
why: More twist lets the top of the main open and spill wind in the gusts.

q: Beating in this breeze, the boat keeps rounding up and you are fighting the wheel. What do you reduce first?
a: Reef the main
why: Weather helm comes from too much drive aft; reducing the main moves it forward.

q: You roll away a third of the genoa as the wind builds. Now the top of the sail luffs early. What do you do with the sheet car?
a: Move it forward
why: Furling moves the clew up and forward, so the lead must follow it forward.

fig.title: Reefed genoa
lines: Car where it was for full sail

q: Broad reaching in a Meltemi with full main, the boat suddenly rounds up and heels hard, the wheel loose in your hands. What was it?
a: A broach: ease the main, then reef
o: A gybe: centre the boom quickly
A broach: sheet the main in hard
why: Too much sail off the wind overpowers the rudder; dump the main, then reduce sail.

fig.title: Broad reach, F6
lines: Rudder losing grip in the gusts

q: After a slow tack the boat has stopped like this and will not turn either way. What is it and what do you do?
a: In irons: back the genoa to push the bow off
o: Hove-to: wait for the wind to shift
In irons: sheet the main in hard
Luffing: steer further into the wind
why: Head to wind with no way on; backing the headsail turns the bow.

q: You want to stop under sail off Poros to sort out a tangled line. How do you heave to?
a: Tack, leave the genoa sheet, lash the helm to turn up
o: Drop both sails and leave the helm free
Gybe and sheet the main in hard
Tack, release the genoa, sheet the main hard
why: The backed genoa and the rudder turning up balance each other; the boat lies quietly.

q: You have hove-to to sort out a jammed reef line. Is this a good place to stay?
a: No: you drift downwind towards the rocks
o: Yes: a hove-to boat makes no leeway
Yes: the backed genoa drives you upwind
No: the boat will tack by itself
why: Hove-to, the boat drifts slowly to leeward; you need sea room downwind.

fig.title: Hove-to
lines: Rocky island 0.5 M to the south

q: Running in a swell, the boom keeps threatening to swing across. What prevents an accidental gybe?
a: Rig a preventer and steer a little higher
o: Pull the traveller up to windward
why: A preventer holds the boom forward, and a broad reach keeps the wind clear of the leech.

q: You need to change to the other broad reach. With this crew, how do you do it?
a: Luff up, tack round, bear away again
o: Gybe with the mainsheet fully eased
Drop the genoa and gybe the main alone
why: In strong wind a tack round avoids a violent gybe; it costs only a little ground.

q: You plan to motor under this bridge. Can you pass?
a: No: your air draft is 17.5 m
why: Air draft is the height of the highest point above the water: 15.5 + 1.2 + 0.8 = 17.5 m.

fig.title: Bridge ahead
lines: VHF aerial on the masthead: 0.8 m

q: Your yacht's figures are below. Roughly what is her maximum speed through the water, short of surfing?
a: About 8 knots
why: Hull speed ≈ 1.34 × √LWL in feet: 1.34 × √36 ≈ 8 knots.

q: This season you move up to a bigger, heavier yacht. Coming into a berth, what changes most?
a: She carries her way longer: slow down earlier
o: She stops sooner because she is heavier
She turns in a much tighter circle
She draws less water at the bow
why: More displacement means more momentum: she takes longer to stop and to start.

q: The bay is 2.0 m deep near the beach. Which of the two charter boats can anchor there?
a: Only the catamaran
why: Draft is the depth of the hull below the waterline; the cat's 1.25 m leaves 0.75 m.

q: The quay attendant offers you this gap. What is the problem?
a: The beam: the cat will not fit
o: The LOA: too long for stern-to
The draft: too deep at the quay
None: cats squeeze in with fenders
why: Beam is the widest point of the boat; a 42 ft cat is about 7.7 m wide.

q: On your catamaran the skipper sends you forward across the netting between the two bows. What is the netting called?
a: The trampoline
why: The trampoline spans the forward beam between the hulls.

q: Beating into a short Meltemi chop, the catamaran shudders with loud bangs under the saloon. What is happening and what do you do?
a: Bridgedeck slamming: bear away and slow down
why: Waves hit the underside of the bridgedeck; a freer, slower course eases it.

q: You swap a monohull for a cruising catamaran on the same upwind leg. What do you expect?
a: She points lower, so you need more tacks
o: She points higher, so fewer tacks
She heels more than the monohull
She tacks faster and more easily
why: A cruising cat without daggerboards sails wider of the wind and makes more leeway.

q: On a cruising catamaran, how do you decide when to reef?
a: By the wind speed, using the reefing table
o: When the windward hull starts to lift
why: A cat barely heels, so it gives no warning; reef by the wind speed.

q: A crew member asks why the catamaran has no heavy keel. Which is true about the stability of the two types?
a: A monohull rights itself; a capsized cat does not
o: Both right themselves after a capsize
A cat rights itself; a monohull does not
A cat heels further than a monohull first
why: The ballast keel brings a monohull back up; an inverted cat is stable upside down.

q: Tacking your charter catamaran in light wind, it keeps stopping head to wind. What helps it round?
a: Build speed, keep the jib backed briefly
o: Slow down and release the jib early
Ease the main fully, then tack
why: A cat carries little way; speed and a backed jib push the bows through.
